This matters because PPO and related algorithms assume a relatively stationary reward signal; if the RM's internal feature weightings drift — say, from penalizing verbosity to rewarding it, because new annotators have different implicit preferences — the policy gradient updates become inconsistent across time, accumulating contradictory parameter updates rather than converging. The concept of preference boundary erosion captures a subtler failure: the decision boundaries separating "preferred" from "dispreferred" responses in the RM's representation space degrade or shift as the training distribution changes, so responses near the boundary get inconsistently labeled across RM versions, creating a noisy and non-stationary reward landscape. Reward landscape topology shifts refer to changes in the global structure of the reward function — not just local boundary perturbations, but the emergence, merger, or disappearance of reward peaks and valleys — which can redirect the policy toward entirely different behavioral modes without any single update appearing catastrophic. What a beginner misses is that these phenomena are largely invisible in aggregate metrics: overall preference accuracy on held-out data can stay flat or improve while feature attribution is silently rotating, so standard RM validation gives no warning that the optimization target has fundamentally changed character.
